title: Comparison sorting: insertion sort vs merge sort
problem_statement: Given a list of n integers, return a new list containing the same elements in non-decreasing order (the input list must not be modified).

input.size_measure: n integers of bounded size; costs are counted in comparisons and element moves, each O(1). The harness draws values uniformly from [-n, n], so duplicates occur.

algorithms.name: insertion sort
algorithms.idea: Grow a sorted prefix one element at a time: shift every larger element of the prefix one place right and drop the new element into the gap.
algorithms.pseudocode: a = copy(xs); for i in 1..n-1: key = a[i]; j = i - 1; while j >= 0 and a[j] > key: a[j+1] = a[j]; j = j - 1; a[j+1] = key; return a
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n + I) where I is the number of inversions: Theta(n^2) in the worst case (reversed input, I = n(n-1)/2) and on average over uniformly random inputs (E[I] ~ n^2/4, the case measured for V2); Theta(n) on sorted input
algorithms.space_complexity: Theta(n) for the output copy, O(1) extra
algorithms.correctness: Invariant: before iteration i, a[0..i-1] holds the first i input elements in sorted order (Knuth TAOCP Vol. 3, 5.2.1; CLRS 2.1).

algorithms.name: merge sort
algorithms.idea: Split the list in half, sort each half recursively, and merge the two sorted halves in one linear pass.
algorithms.pseudocode: sort(xs): if |xs| <= 1 return copy(xs); L = sort(left half); R = sort(right half); return merge(L, R)
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n log n) on every input: T(n) = 2 T(n/2) + Theta(n)
algorithms.correctness: Induction on n: merging two sorted lists by repeatedly taking the smaller head yields a sorted list of all their elements (Knuth TAOCP Vol. 3, 5.2.4; CLRS 2.3).

relationship: Insertion sort removes one inversion per element move, and a random list has Theta(n^2) of them. Merge sort's divide and conquer reaches Theta(n log n), which is optimal for comparison sorting.

sources.title: The Art of Computer Programming, Vol. 3: Sorting and Searching (2nd ed.)
sources.note: Section 5.2.1 (sorting by insertion), 5.2.4 (sorting by merging), 5.3.1 (minimum-comparison sorting: the log2(n!) lower bound, worst case and average).

sources.authors: Cormen, T. H.; Leiserson, C. E.; Rivest, R. L.; Stein, C.
sources.title: Introduction to Algorithms (3rd ed.)
sources.note: Chapter 2 (insertion sort, merge sort) and section 8.1 (lower bounds for sorting).

sources.title: Integer sorting in O(n sqrt(log log n)) expected time and linear space

verification.method: V1: both implementations agree with each other and with Python's built-in sorted() (used only as the oracle) on random lists from [-n, n], n = 0..5, 8, 16, 50, 100, 500 and 2000; the validator also checks that neither mutates its input. V2: on uniformly random lists, runtimes fit n^2 (insertion sort, average case, n = 100..3200) and n log n (merge sort, n = 1000..64000). At the default tolerance 0.25 a fit against n alone would also pass for merge sort (the log factor changes the slope by only ~0.1 over this range), so V2 confirms near-linear growth rather than isolating the log factor.

lower_bounds.bound: Omega(n log n) comparisons: at least log2(n!) = n log2 n - O(n) in the worst case, and also on average over a uniformly random input order, hence in expectation for any randomized comparison sort
lower_bounds.setting: comparison model (elements are accessed only through pairwise comparisons)
lower_bounds.source: Knuth TAOCP Vol. 3 (1998), 5.3.1 (decision-tree argument, worst and average case); the randomized case follows from the average case by Yao's minimax principle

caveats: The Omega(n log n) lower bound holds only in the comparison model. Integers can be sorted faster by exploiting their representation (e.g. radix sort in O(n w / log n) for w-bit keys, or Han-Thorup O(n sqrt(log log n)) expected time on a word RAM), so merge sort is optimal among comparison sorts, not for integer sorting in general. Insertion sort's cost depends on the input: it is linear on (nearly) sorted lists, which is why practical hybrids such as Timsort use it on short runs. V2 measures insertion sort's average case (random input), which is Theta(n^2), the same order as its worst case.
notes: The classic textbook T3 pair. Merge sort is usually credited to John von Neumann (1945).
